title: Frequently Asked Questions
subhead: Common questions about MAPLE, testimony, MAPLE's tools, accounts, and privacy.
ctaBody: If you don't see what you're looking for, please reach out with any questions.

qAndA.question: Is MAPLE part of the state legislature or government?
qAndA.answer: No. MAPLE is an independent project of Partners in Democracy - Education, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It is not affiliated with the Massachusetts Legislature or any other part of state government.

qAndA.question: What is MAPLE trying to accomplish?
qAndA.answer: MAPLE helps Massachusetts residents and organizations take part in making state law: finding and following bills, writing and submitting testimony, and reading what others have said. Testimony shared on MAPLE stays in a public, searchable archive. Under the Legislature's joint rules for the 2025–2026 session, committees must make the written testimony they receive public, but each committee decides how, and the Legislature is exempt from the state's public records and open meeting laws. MAPLE aims to make more of the process visible in one place.

qAndA.question: What is a “nonprofit digital public space”?
qAndA.answer: Most online conversation about politics happens on commercial platforms such as Facebook and X, which are designed to hold attention and earn a profit. MAPLE is a nonprofit space built for a different purpose: civil, substantive discussion of proposed laws, and a direct way to bring residents' knowledge and views to their elected representatives.

qAndA.question: How else is MAPLE different from social media?
qAndA.answer: We don't sell your data, and we don't rank posts to maximize engagement. You choose which bills, organizations and conference committees to follow, and your newsfeed shows their updates newest first. The focus stays on the proposed laws that shape our lives.

qAndA.question: Does posting testimony on MAPLE submit it to the Legislature?
qAndA.answer: Not by itself. Publishing on MAPLE shares your testimony publicly on MAPLE. When you publish, MAPLE also drafts an email with your testimony, addressed to the committee hearing the bill, in your own email program. Sending that email is how you submit it to the committee. We can't guarantee that legislators will see testimony that appears only on MAPLE. Committees set their own procedures for receiving testimony, and some hearings also accept it through the Legislature's website, so check the hearing notice on [malegislature.gov](https://malegislature.gov) for the committee's instructions.

qAndA.question: Will the Legislature make my testimony public?
qAndA.answer: Under the Legislature's joint rules for the 2025–2026 session, committees must make the written testimony they receive publicly available, and each committee decides how. Testimony you publish on MAPLE is public on MAPLE either way.

qAndA.question: How do I edit my testimony?
qAndA.answer: Go to your profile, click “Edit Profile”, open the “Testimonies” tab, and choose the testimony you want to edit. MAPLE keeps and displays earlier versions of testimony you've published and edited.

qAndA.question: Can I delete my testimony?
qAndA.answer: Generally, no. We do allow deletion in some circumstances, such as testimony posted with personal or sensitive information, or posted on the wrong bill. To request a deletion, email [admin@mapletestimony.org](mailto:admin@mapletestimony.org).

qAndA.question: What can I follow on MAPLE?
qAndA.answer: You can follow bills, organizations and conference committees. Updates from what you follow appear in your [newsfeed](/newsfeed), newest first.

qAndA.question: Can MAPLE email me updates?
qAndA.answer: Yes. In your profile settings, you can choose to get email updates about the bills and organizations you follow, daily, weekly or monthly, or turn them off.

qAndA.question: Why can't I see follower counts?
qAndA.answer: Public profiles don't show how many followers someone has. We think follower counts encourage performance rather than sincerity. You can see your own followers on your Edit Profile page.

qAndA.question: What are MAPLE's hearing transcripts?
qAndA.answer: MAPLE publishes video and time-stamped, searchable transcripts of Massachusetts legislative committee hearings, where they are available. Transcripts are produced automatically with speech-recognition software, so they can contain errors. Find them on the [Hearings](/hearings) page.

qAndA.question: What is the Lobbying Explorer?
qAndA.answer: The [Lobbying Explorer](/lobbying) shows who registered to lobby Massachusetts state government, on what, and for whom, as they reported it to the Secretary of the Commonwealth. You can follow links to the original disclosures on the Secretary's website.

qAndA.question: What are the conference committee pages?
qAndA.answer: When the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee of six legislators negotiates the final text. MAPLE's [conference committee pages](/conferences) show who is negotiating and what is still being worked out, and let you share your input.

qAndA.question: Does MAPLE use AI?
qAndA.answer: In some features. See [How MAPLE uses AI](/about/how-maple-uses-ai) for where and how.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between “organization” and “individual” accounts?
qAndA.answer: MAPLE has two account types: organization and individual. We verify organizations (corporations, LLCs, LPs and so on) with the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth. This helps us fight trolling and spam, and lets readers trust that organization testimony is authentic. Organizations speak for many people, so MAPLE gives their testimony more prominence in some places. Individual accounts can be public or private (see below); organization accounts are always public.

qAndA.question: Does my group qualify for an organization account?
qAndA.answer: If your group isn't formally registered with the Secretary of the Commonwealth, such as a student or neighborhood group, please sign up for an individual account. We plan to add more account types in the future.

qAndA.question: What does it mean to have a “private” or “public” account?
qAndA.answer: Individuals can make their profile public or private. On a public profile, your name links to a profile page showing all your testimony and any bio or social media links you've added. On a private profile, your name isn't a link and there's no public profile page.

qAndA.question: How is my personal information treated?
qAndA.answer: Information you share on MAPLE is displayed publicly, and we don't sell user data. Other than login credentials, we don't keep user-provided information private. Read more in our [Privacy Policy](/policies/privacy).

qAndA.question: Can I delete my account?
qAndA.answer: Because a core function of MAPLE is to preserve and archive testimony, we don't currently allow users to delete their profiles.

qAndA.question: Should I use my real name on MAPLE?
qAndA.answer: We encourage it. Legislators give more weight to testimony when they can verify that you're a constituent, and journalists and researchers may want to cite your testimony or contact you about it. You can leave some details out of what you post on MAPLE: for example, you could leave your address out of your MAPLE post and still include it in the email you send to the committee.

qAndA.question: How can I report testimony?
qAndA.answer: Every published testimony has a “Report” link. Click it, and you'll be asked for some basic information about why you're reporting it.

qAndA.question: How does moderation work?
qAndA.answer: Our moderators review reported testimony. Testimony that violates our [Code of Conduct](/policies/code-of-conduct) may be removed at the moderators' discretion, and they may also freeze the account that posted it. Review can take a few days.

qAndA.question: Who are the moderators?
qAndA.answer: A team of Massachusetts-based moderators trained by MAPLE reviews testimony published on MAPLE. The moderators include volunteer members of the MAPLE team.

qAndA.question: Who is behind MAPLE?
qAndA.answer: MAPLE is an initiative of Partners in Democracy - Education, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It was co-founded by Matthew Victor and Nathan Sanders, developed in partnership with Northeastern University School of Law's NuLawLab, and built in the open with Code for Boston volunteers. Matthew is MAPLE's only staff member; everyone else on the team volunteers. [Meet the team](/about/our-team).

qAndA.question: How can I support MAPLE?
qAndA.answer: There are lots of ways: share feedback, volunteer with us, help MAPLE grow, or contribute financially. See [Support MAPLE](/about/support-maple) for details.

qAndA.question: Who do I contact to learn more?
qAndA.answer: Email us at [admin@mapletestimony.org](mailto:admin@mapletestimony.org).
